title: Vayechi: twelve blessings (Genesis 49)
hookLine: each son receives a different blessing, fitted to who he is

lines: THE WORDS ONLY YOU COULD GET.
cards: One teacher wrote the same comment on every report card. Pleasure to have in class. Nice.
Harmless. And forgettable, because it wasn't about you.

Then there's the teacher who said something only you could have received: the thing that stung a little and was true, or the thing that saw a gift nobody else had noticed. You probably still remember the words.
Jacob is on his deathbed, his twelve sons crowded around. And he doesn't give one blessing twelve times.

teach.h: A LION, A HARBOR, A DEER, A WOLF.
teach.b: Genesis forty-nine is a long poem, one of the oldest-sounding passages in the Torah, and its Hebrew is well known for it, hard. Jacob goes son by son, and every word is different. Judah is a young lion.
Zebulun will live by the shore, a harbor for ships. Issachar is a strong donkey, bending his shoulder to work. Naphtali is a deer running free.
Benjamin is a wolf. Not every word is sweet. Reuben, the firstborn, is told he's unstable as water, and he loses first place.

Simeon and Levi hear their father curse their anger, the violence they did years before. Then the Torah sums it up, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "every one according to his blessing he blessed them."
Each one, his own. Rashi notices the word them at the end.
Even Reuben, Simeon and Levi, the ones who got hard words, were blessed.

A true blessing can include the truth. Other commentators point out that the lion, the harbor, the deer are about what each son is suited for: leadership, trade, work, speed. Jacob isn't handing out prizes.
He's naming who each one is, and sending him toward it. Every family, every office, every classroom has its twelve different children.

The Torah's picture of a blessing isn't one warm sentence for the group chat. It's attention: looking long enough at one person to know their particular strength and their particular danger, and saying so with love.

how: Jacob's twelve sons became the twelve tribes of Israel, and images from these blessings, such as Judah's lion and Naphtali's deer, still appear on synagogue windows, Torah covers and Jewish art.

o: and he lived, the last portion in the book of Genesis
and he spoke, Jacob's poem for his twelve sons
and he wandered, the story of the desert years

games.q: each son, his own image — tap the pairs.
p: by the shore, a harbor for ships

s: Jacob gave every son the same blessing
each son got different words: every one according to his blessing.
some of the sons got hard words, not praise
Reuben, Simeon and Levi were rebuked. Rashi says they were still blessed.
Genesis 49 is written as a poem
it's one of the long poems of the Torah, and its Hebrew is notoriously hard.

games.q: you're Jacob, dying, with twelve very different sons at your bed. how do you bless them?
o: one warm blessing for all twelve together.
different words for each son, some of them hard.
only the sons who treated you well.
games.why: Jacob spoke to each son separately, with images fitted to each, and rebukes for three. the Torah says he blessed every one according to his blessing.

practice: Bring to mind two people you care about who are nothing alike, and ask of the first: what is their particular strength, their lion, their harbor?
Find a wish that fits only them, then do the same for the second; not speeches, just two honest, different wishes.
